zones.label: Column 1

lines.note: Geinō, yoi shiwaza, is introduced as the liberal arts. The headword's long o has a circumflex; the geographical qualification follows.
These are the arts of Japan or China; gei then introduces rei, gaku and sha. The unusual mark in Gùeiua and the close ouda spacing are retained provisionally from this impression.
Gyo, sho and su complete the six arts. Their Portuguese equivalents begin with civilized conduct, music and shooting; Policia is wholly italic, not the OCR's mixed-font word.

runs.text: arco, arte de caualgar, de eſcreuer, & cõtar.

lines.note: Completes shooting with a bow, then riding, writing and counting. The six Portuguese glosses correspond in order to the Japanese list above.
Nō introduces kin, gi, sho and ga: instrumental music, the board game, writing and painting, elaborated below. This Japanese list is not embedded Portuguese prose.
Explains playing a musical instrument, especially one likened to a cravo. The dictionary's analogy is retained without asserting an exact modern instrument identification.

runs.text: arte de jugar o go, eſcreuer, e pintar.

lines.note: The remaining accomplishments are playing go, writing and painting. Go is Japanese vocabulary occurring within an otherwise Portuguese explanation.
Geisai is glossed as arts and knowledge. The long s in the headword is retained as printed rather than modernized.
Geisha is here gei aru mono, a person possessing arts or skills. The gloss concerns an accomplished person, not a later occupational definition.
Completes the description as someone who knows arts or has abilities. This is the continuation of Gueixa.
Gejigeji names a creature said to suck and pull out hair. This records the dictionary's account, not a verified zoological claim.
The hair is said to be removed without pain. This completes the description of the creature in the preceding row.

runs.text: Hum inſtrumento de bambu com que

lines.note: Gejiki first denotes a bamboo implement. The relative clause below explains its use for removing hair.

runs.text: arrancaõ os cabelos da cabeça os

lines.note: Japanese people use the implement to pluck hair from the head. The scan places the tilde on the final o of arrancaõ, which is preserved.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Hum certo bicho que por ſi arranca

lines.note: A second sense identifies a creature that itself removes hair. The visible paragraph mark before Item was omitted by OCR and has been restored.

runs.text: eſtes cabelos de noite eſtando hum dormindo.

lines.note: The creature supposedly removes hair at night while the person sleeps. The line continues the source's description rather than introducing an actual medical assertion.
The upper-region name is gejigeji. Both Cami and Guejigueji occur inside the Portuguese regional explanation and qualify for whole-word typeface review.
The verb gejiki is labelled low or vulgar usage and means squandering goods. The printed principal parts, including ijta, are preserved rather than expanded into modern inflections.
Completes wasting property, then gives gejiki ushinō as the example. The scan supports initial G, not C; Gas- begins its Portuguese translation.
Completes gastar and explains wasting all one's property or goods. The word is fato, with f, not OCR ſato.
Gejō, shiro yori oruru, means coming down from or surrendering a fortress. The headword begins G rather than OCR C.

runs.text: taleza, ou entregala a os inimigos rendendoſe.

lines.note: Completes fortaleza and specifies handing it to the enemy by surrendering. The printed separation a os is retained.
Gejun is the last ten days of the month, paraphrased tsuki no owari no tōka. Here the o in tôca has an upward-pointing circumflex, unlike the preceding headword's caron.
Radeiros completes derradeiros: the final ten days of the month. This finishes the Guejun entry.
Gen is paraphrased arawaruru, to become manifest. The short Portuguese gloss gives the reflexive manifestar-se.

runs.text: Sinal, ou effeito dalgũa couſa como de

lines.note: A second gen means a sign or effect, illustrated by recovery from disease. The tilde in dalgũa is preserved on u.
The example concerns illness being cured and introduces Kiyomori. The Japanese proper name starts the quotation continued below.
The quotation says that various prayers were performed, but their effect did not follow. The scan supports xeraretaredomo, replacing OCR's c in the concessive ending; so- continues into sono.

Completes sono gen ga nakatta, there was no effect. Fei. is the roman citation label; lib. and its following i-like book indicator are italic. Qiyomori begins the Portuguese translation and is also italic here.

runs.text: fez varias deprecaçoens, &c. mas não oui

lines.note: The translation says Kiyomori made various supplications, but there was no result. The damaged final verb is read provisionally as ouu.; ouue is expected linguistically, but a final e is not securely visible and has not been supplied.

runs.text: ſinal nem effeito, ou melhoria da doença.

lines.note: There was no sign, effect or improvement in the illness. This completes the negative result of the prayers in the quoted example.
Gena is a particle added after other words. The scan supports ajunta rather than ajuita; postpo- continues across the line break.
Completes postpoem, describing placement after other words, then gives maitta gena. The following gloss interprets it as an appearance or report of arrival.
Maitta gena is translated as apparently he came; wakai gena begins a parallel example about being young. The joined Pareceque is retained as printed.
Completes parece que he mancebo, apparently he is a young man. This finishes the second example of Guena.

runs.text: Por nome de homem aos mininos,

lines.note: Genbuku is explained as giving boys an adult male name. The next row supplies the accompanying first wearing of a sword.

runs.text: & fazer lhes cingir Catana a primeira vez.

lines.note: The boys are made to gird on a katana for the first time. Catana is a Japanese noun embedded in the Portuguese explanation.
Genbutxa describes a hotoke who responds promptly. Fotoque is embedded in Portuguese, and depreßa retains the source's double-s sort.

runs.text: & ouue as petiçoens, ou dà logo premio, ou

lines.note: The figure hears petitions or immediately gives a reward or the contrasting outcome below. This continues the description of responsiveness.
Castigo supplies punishment as the alternative to reward. The source's st-type is retained without imposing a global long-s classification.
Genkan is severe cold, paraphrased kibishii samushi. The final S. is a roman written-register label, not part of the italic Portuguese gloss.
Genjū means justice and severity. The headword's u-mark points upward; the example uses abbreviated Guẽ- and continues on the next row.

Completes genjū ni shōbatsu wo okonō, administering rewards or punishment strictly. Reinspection supports a grave-like stroke over u here, so giùni is retained rather than harmonized with the circumflex in the headword Guengiû above.
Completes the giving of punishment or reward rightly and severely. The historical recta is left in the source's adverbial construction.
This genjū is kaeri sumu, returning to live in one's home place. Its u-mark points downward, distinguishing the printed headword from the preceding Guengiû despite identical modern vowel length.

runs.text: ou do desterro habitar ẽ ſua terra. Vt,

lines.note: The return may be from exile to residence in one's native land. The scan reads habitar and abbreviated Guẽ-, rather than babitar and Cue-.
Completes genjū itasu, to make that return and resume residence. The caron and long s in itaſu are retained.
Genjū na describes a righteous, just and severe person. The damaged initial retains traces consistent with G, not the OCR's iu; the u-mark here is kept as a grave.
Gengyō is paraphrased arawaruru katachi, an appearing or manifest form. The Portuguese begins with figure or thing.
Completes a thing that appears, then says the enemy has appeared. Printed itaita is retained as a historical inflection rather than modernized to itashita.

runs.text: Ia osinimigos aparecerão, ou estão deſcuber-

lines.note: The enemies have appeared or are now exposed. The close osinimigos spacing is retained; descubertos continues across the line break.
Completes discovered, then gives toga gengyō shita, a fault becoming manifest. The Portuguese translation starts with Descu-.
Completes descubriose o peccado: the sin or offence was revealed. This is the translation of the preceding Japanese example.
Guenguio is explained through kotoba and kataru and glossed simply as a word or speech. Its unmarked final o is not assimilated to the preceding Guenguiǒ.

runs.text: Hũ genero de traue que ſerue nos

lines.note: A homonymous Guenguio is a kind of structural beam. The abbreviated Hũ is retained without expanding hum.
The beam is used in buildings and houses. This completes the architectural sense of Guenguio.

runs.text: O que faz milagres, ou obras de vir-

lines.note: Genja is someone who performs miracles or works of power or virtue. Vir- continues into virtude below.
Completes virtude and adds wondrous works. The definition describes the figure through acts attributed to him.
Genze means this world, as opposed to another life or realm. The locally printed Este is retained without a global st/ſt change.
Genzen is paraphrased as appearing before someone. The final Portuguese word Aparecer continues into its directional complement below.
Diante completes appearing in front. The final S. is the roman label for written usage, not part of the gloss.
Genji is the Minamoto lineage, described as a renowned family. The scan supports initial G rather than C; the unusual Portuguese accent and spelling are preserved.
Completes nomeada and calls the lineage old in Japan. This finishes the family-name entry, distinct from the book-title entry below.

runs.text: Hũs certos liuros poeticos de his-

lines.note: This Genji denotes a set of literary or poetic narrative books. The visible G corrects OCR C; the historical Hũs abbreviation is retained.
Torias completes historias, finishing the literary definition. The source does not spell out a longer title on this row.
Genji, genzuru, genjita is the verb to manifest or reveal. Qi- begins kidoku in the following example; the principal parts remain in their printed abbreviated form.
Kidoku wo genzuru means manifesting wonders or miraculous effects. The Portuguese gloss begins making or manifesting, divided at the row ending.
Tar completes manifestar milagres, to manifest miracles. This completes the example under the first Guenji verb.
The second genji verb means diminishing or losing material. It is a distinct entry despite the identical printed principal parts.
The loss is illustrated by silver when melted. This explains quebrar as reduction or wastage rather than only physically breaking an object.
Genjōraku is a particular musical piece or ensemble performance. The following line specifies many instruments together; no more precise modern title is imposed.
Many instruments play together, completing the description of Genjōraku. The printed instrumentos and juntos remain separate Portuguese words.
Geni and genigeni are adverbs meaning reasonably, truly or indeed. The scan supports initial G rather than C; Latin l introduces the alternative.
Ou de verdade adds in truth as the alternative gloss. This continues the preceding adverb entry.
Genimo is another adverb glossed com rezão, with reason or indeed. The damaged internal strokes do not justify changing the headword.
Genin, shita no hito, denotes a servant or a person in service. The Portuguese peßoa retains its historical double-s sort.
Serviço completes the person-of-service definition. The opening is long s, and the entire short continuation is italic.
Genmit is equated with genjū and means rigorous or strict. The scan supports G in Guengiǔ; its locally printed caron is not replaced to match another occurrence.
Completes strict and correct, then gives genmit ni ōsetsukerareta, an order delivered rigorously. The circumflex in vôxetçuqerareta is retained.
The Portuguese says the order was given rigorously and correctly. This completes the example under Guenmit.
Genmu combines maboroshi and yume, an illusion or dream. The gloss describes a vain or fleeting dream.
The dream lasts only a short time. Bup. is a roman Buddhist usage label and has been separated from the italic gloss.

runs.text: Guen, ni, bi, jet, xin, y.

lines.note: Gen, ni, bi, zet, shin and i enumerate the six sensory faculties. The final t in jet and the single-letter y are retained as printed.
The dictionary attributes this sixfold classification to Chinese and Japanese usage. S. is roman; Ma- starts the Japanese explanatory list with manako.

runs.text: naco, mimi, fana, xita, mi, cocoro.

lines.note: Completes manako and lists eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body and mind. These are standalone Japanese equivalents, not embedded Portuguese terms for font toggling.

runs.text: Ver, ouuir, cheirar, gostar, palpar, ſenti-

lines.note: The Portuguese maps the list to seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching, then begins the final faculty. The original gostar spelling and line-end senti- are retained.
Do completes sentido comum, the dictionary's term for the final mental faculty. It should not be reduced to the modern everyday sense of good judgment.
Gen ni kō enumerates eyes, ears and mouth, also given as manako, mimi and kuchi. The printed spacing in Guen nicô is retained rather than resegmented.
Ears and mouth complete the Portuguese equivalent list. This short continuation belongs to Guen nicô.

Gennin, maboroshi no hito, describes human existence as illusory. The line's final ha is anomalous before mana below, where humana is expected; the visible reading is retained rather than silently repaired.

runs.text: mana miſerauel, & de pouca dura. S.

lines.note: Completes the description of miserable, short-lived human nature. The ha/mana division above is preserved with its caveat; S. is a roman written-register label.
Genpu, kaeri tsuku, means returning or being restored. The Portuguese continuation specifies the former income or status.
The restoration is to one's previous revenue or position. Genpu starts the Japanese example completed on the next physical row.
Genpu serareta means having been restored to the former position. The dictionary's xerareta spelling is retained, and the separate catchword below is not body text.
